_comment: Sensors with no machine-readable feed. Updated by research, not by fetch.py. Each carries its own 'asof' date; the dashboard marks anything older than 45 days as stale so a forgotten sensor cannot quietly pass for a current reading. state: 0 calm, 1 watch, 2 turning.

A4.value: all three raise 2027; capacity sold out
A4.detail: The Q3 calls are in and none of the four large buyers used cautious language. Microsoft (2026-10-28): Azure +48%, guided to 49-50% next quarter; capex of $45.2bn came in below plan because third-party GPU suppliers delivered late, pushing capacity into H1 2027 — a supply complaint, which Rule 05 reads as the opposite of a warning; Q2 capex above $50bn, about $170bn for the calendar year; commercial RPO +73% to $677bn. Alphabet (2026-10-28): Google Cloud +103% to $30.7bn, backlog $561bn, Q3 capex about $51.4bn, 2026 range held at $195-205bn and 'we continue to expect our capex to increase significantly in 2027'. Amazon (2026-10-29): AWS +39%, its fastest in nearly five years, backlog $578bn, capacity 'largely sold out' for next year, 2026 capex about $220bn and 2027 'meaningfully more'. Meta (2026-10-21) raised the floor of its range. The market punished all of it (Alphabet about -10%, Amazon about -7% after hours), but the share price is not this sensor's question: the words are still 'we cannot build fast enough'.
A4.source: Microsoft FY2027 Q1 release and call (2026-10-28); Alphabet Q3 2026 release and call, CNBC and Fortune (2026-10-28); Amazon Q3 2026 release and call, CNBC and GeekWire (2026-10-29); Meta Q3 2026 (2026-10-21)

B2.detail: The H1 2026 surveys published in September are still the latest: CBRE primary-market vacancy a record 1.4% (Northern Virginia 0.2%), JLL North America about 1% for the third year running, 25 GW absorbed in H1 and most tenants now contracting for 2028 deliveries. JLL counts 66 GW under construction, 95% pre-committed. Nothing points to space coming free; the next reading is the year-end round in February and March.
B2.source: CBRE North America Data Center Trends H1 2026 (2026-09-08); JLL North America Data Center Report midyear 2026

B3.value: record build, cancellations doubling, for local reasons
B3.detail: Construction is still at a record — CBRE 7,481 MW under way in the primary markets, +24.8% in H1. The cancellation half keeps clustering: Uptime Institute counts 26 cancelled giant campuses in H1 2026 against 12 in all of 2025, Data Center Watch 45 US projects worth about $68bn blocked or delayed in Q2 after about $130bn in Q1, and New York stopped taking proposals for large new facilities in July. Rule 05 holds: the stated reasons are local opposition, power and permits, not tenants walking away. Watch, not turning, because construction is rising, not down 15%.
B3.source: CBRE H1 2026; Uptime Institute Update 528 (September 2026); Data Center Watch Q2 2026; Heatmap cancellation tracking

C1.value: lenders push back on the most-indebted builders
C1.detail: The volume has kept rising: Barclays counts $346bn of capital raised by hyperscalers, data-centre operators and neoclouds so far in 2026, against $172bn for all of 2025. The new part is the lender side, which since mid-October has started to refuse the weakest borrowers. CoreWeave's five-year CDS went above 1,100bp (CNBC, 2026-10-15) and its unsecured bonds yield about 15%; Oracle's spread was 308bp on 2026-10-21 against 141bp on 2026-01-02; SoftBank's CDS is near a four-year high above 420bp; Meta's CDS is reported at a record of about 115bp; a Korean neocloud IPO failed (PitchBook). Evercore's desk sums up the market's line as no more AI debt without operating cash flow behind it, and Huang publicly called capital 'scarce'. Still watch, not turning: the turn needs most new spending to be borrowed, and the five large buyers still pay most of it from cash (see A2). But this is the sensor closest to turning, and the stress sits exactly where the thesis expects it: with the companies that build on borrowed money rather than with the cash-rich hyperscalers. C2 cannot see this, because it measures the whole high-yield market. Update 2026-10-28: the repricing has reached the large names. Oracle's five-year CDS widened to about 315bp (2026-10-19, up about 300% on a year), and Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia CDS are reported at record wides, though far below Oracle's. CoreWeave eased slightly to about 1,080bp. Oracle plans about $40bn of debt and equity this fiscal year after negative free cash flow of $5.4bn last quarter. Still watch: the cash-rich buyers still fund most capex themselves, but the board's automatic credit readings now confirm the move (E1 turning, C2 on watch). Update 2026-10-29: the Q3 reports show the cash cover thinning at the cash-rich buyers too: Alphabet's free cash flow was about -$9.1bn in Q3 and its long-term debt rose to $125.1bn; Amazon's trailing free cash flow swung to an outflow of $42.4bn. A2 (capex against operating cash flow, median of the five) rose to 89% with the new filings. Still watch: the buyers still pay most capex from operating cash, but the margin is close to used up.
C1.source: CNBC on CoreWeave CDS (2026-10-15) and Oracle spreads (2026-10-21/22); Barclays research via Yahoo Finance (October 2026); PitchBook on the Korean neocloud IPO; CNBC Huang interview (2026-10-22); CNBC on Oracle and CoreWeave credit (2026-10-19); 24/7 Wall St. on record bond sales (2026-10-27); Alphabet and Amazon Q3 2026 results (2026-10-28/29)

C3.detail: Checked in the filings themselves: the Q3 10-Qs of Microsoft (filed 2026-10-28), Alphabet (2026-10-29) and Meta (2026-10-22) disclose no change in the useful life of servers or network equipment and no write-down of AI hardware; useful lives appear only in the standard list of estimates. Alphabet's filing adds the generic caution that technology advances could change the period over which assets are depreciated. The standing picture holds: Alphabet six years for servers, Microsoft two to six, Meta 5.5 years after stretching (2025), Amazon the one to have shortened a subset from six to five; Microsoft's longer life for buildings (15 to 25 years) applies from this quarter. Watch stays because the earlier stretches stand, not because of anything new. Amazon's 10-Q is still to come.
C3.source: Microsoft 10-Q (2026-10-28), Alphabet 10-Q (2026-10-29), Meta 10-Q (2026-10-22), read on EDGAR; 2025 10-K useful-life disclosures

C4.value: $308bn, $212bn, $159bn: two falls, both from the two labs
C4.detail: Global venture funding fell for a second quarter, to $159bn in Q3 from $212bn in Q2 and $308bn in Q1 (Crunchbase), which meets the letter of the turn. Read as the sensor's note asks, it does not meet the substance: Q1 held $188bn in four rounds (OpenAI $122bn, Anthropic $30bn, xAI $20bn, Waymo $16bn), and without OpenAI and Anthropic the quarters run roughly $156bn, $147bn, $159bn — flat to up. Q3 was +53% year on year, AI took $102bn (64%), and a record 27 companies raised $1bn or more. No reporting of ratchets, preference stacks or down rounds at the large labs. Raised to watch because the headline now falls and the next lab round decides the direction; scored turning only if amounts fall without the mega-round explanation or terms harden. Update 2026-10-23: no new quarterly figure (Q4 data comes in early January), but the terms side is hardening at the edge: a Korean neocloud IPO failed in October and Huang called capital 'scarce' for neoclouds. These are public markets and credit, not venture rounds, so they do not move the sensor yet; the next lab round decides. Update 2026-10-28: Anthropic filed its IPO prospectus publicly on 2026-10-26: revenue of about $16.3bn in H1 2026 against $1.2bn a year earlier, an offering reported at $100bn or more at a $1.5-2tn valuation. A public listing of that size is the opposite of a funding window closing, so the substance of this sensor eases; the headline fall in venture amounts stays, hence still watch until the Q4 figures in January.
C4.source: Crunchbase News Q3 2026 global funding report (early October 2026); Crunchbase Q1 and H1 2026 data; PitchBook (October 2026); CNBC Huang interview (2026-10-22); Anthropic S-1 as reported by CNBC, Axios and Investing.com (2026-10-26)

D1.detail: The turn the September reading expected has come. Smartphones fell 6.7% in Q2 (IDC) and about 20% in Q3 (Counterpoint, preliminary; the lowest third quarter since 2012) — two quarters beyond -5%. PCs fell 20.1% to 62.7m in Q3 after a revised -3.8% in Q2 (IDC). China alone fell 15.4%, its sixth straight decline. Every source names the same cause: memory and component costs pushing up shelf prices. The caveat for PCs is real — IDC says buyers stocked up early in the year ahead of price rises, borrowing from H2 — but the phone decline has no such pull-in behind it, and IDC expects the next few quarters to get worse before they improve. IDC's own global phone figure for Q3 is still due.
D1.source: IDC PC tracker Q3 2026 (2026-10-08); IDC China smartphone Q3 2026 (2026-10-13); Counterpoint global smartphone Q3 2026 preliminary; IDC Q2 2026

D4.value: AI seats and ARR still expanding
D4.detail: The large sellers still report expansion, not cancellation. Salesforce (Q2 FY2027, 2026-08-26) put Agentforce ARR above $1.5bn, up over 240%, and AI plus Data 360 near $3.9bn — flattered by a wider definition from this quarter. Microsoft 365 Copilot went from 15m paid seats in January to about 30m by the June quarter, with net adds more than doubling. Against that: surveys of mid-market buyers describe 2026 as the year 2024-25 AI commitments meet real usage data, and only a minority report the returns they bought for. That is anecdote and forecast, which the sensor caps at watch, and no seller has reported a cancellation wave. Update 2026-10-29: the order books say expansion, not cancellation: Microsoft commercial remaining performance obligations +73% to $677bn, Google Cloud backlog $561bn, AWS backlog $578bn (more than doubled in a year) with capacity largely sold out for 2027. Backlogs are commitments, not usage, and include the large labs (see C5), but no seller reports cancellations.
D4.source: Salesforce Q2 FY2027 results; Microsoft FY2026 Q3/Q4 calls; RBC CIO survey and renewal commentary (2026); Q3 2026 results of Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon (2026-10-28/29)

C5.value: vendors fund and guarantee their own buyers
C5.detail: The chip sellers have become lenders to the people who buy their chips. Nvidia is putting about $30bn into OpenAI and guaranteeing up to $105bn for an OpenAI-leased campus in Ohio (figures differ between reports), and in August set up a platform with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to raise more than $500bn for chip buyers, offering residual-value support of up to 25% per deal. AMD effectively guarantees a $300m Goldman loan to Crusoe that is secured on AMD chips. GPU-backed loans are now routine (CoreWeave $8.5bn in March, secured on chips plus a Meta contract). The buyer at the centre runs about $50bn of annual revenue against compute plans reported at $600bn to 2030, cut from about $1.4tn. Watch, not turning: no guarantee has been called and no vendor-financed buyer has missed a payment. The cut in OpenAI's plan is the thing to follow; a renegotiated contract with a vendor would be the turn. Update 2026-10-28: Anthropic's prospectus shows the same pattern at the second large lab: compute commitments tallied at roughly $570-650bn (Google up to $114.5bn to 2033, Amazon at least $110bn to 2036, SpaceX's compute unit up to $120.5bn to 2029) against H1 revenue of $16.3bn. The two labs together carry well over $1tn of commitments to a handful of vendors. Still watch: nothing has been called or renegotiated.
C5.source: Yahoo Finance and The Conversation on Nvidia's OpenAI and Ohio commitments (Aug-Oct 2026); Nvidia financing platform announcement (August 2026); DCD on AMD and Crusoe; Bloomberg Law on CoreWeave's GPU loan; DCD on OpenAI's revised compute plan; Anthropic S-1 coverage (Benzinga, Axios, Investing.com, 2026-10-26)
